What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found something through a friend of a friend, no I was lucky. If you have connections in Oslo, I think it's doable, but if you don't, I imagine it would be a bit difficult.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Almost every international student lives in student housing, so there is definitively I large social aspect to it (especially at Sogn). But I didn't feel like I missed out on much, as I made a lot of friends who lived at Sogn and was still included in social things. Personally, I liked not living in a shared apartment with 6 other people. 
I think it was a plus to move into a furnished apartment that has almost everything I needed, so I didn't have to buy too much in the beginning (there was a big struggle to buy drying racks in the first week, bc it was sold out everywhere). It felt more like a home, while I think some of my friend who lived in student housing didn't have the same feeling about their place.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to pre-register for courses, but then sign up for them later. It was super confusing.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They were really good at answering emails and you could even go talk to the personnel on campus.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very, I had to go with my plan D or something.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register for a lot of courses and try to plan out the timetables before you go. It will make the first weeks less stressful.

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: One course was great, the other was incredibly difficult.

questions.answer: Pretty similar.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Fungal biology, molecular mechanism in intracellular signalling.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Fungal biology! It is not super relevant for my studies (biochemistry), but it was a really great course. The teachers were so motivated and nice. There's a field trip in the first month, so you get the know the other students really well, both international and Norwegians. And it was super fun. Even the exam was so relaxed and comfortable, even though I didn't do super well.

questions.answer: So many, the associations day was great to explore all of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The photoclub was fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on all the hikes and trips. Not necessarily though ESN, we planned it on our own and it was really great.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, but I am half Norwegian, so it was pretty natural for me.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I was super lucky to meet some amazing people in my Buddy Group. There are so many opportunities to meet people, so just be open and remember that everyone else is just as nervous as you. Especially the international students are super eager to meet new friends. They have a lot of clubs, associations and sports you can join, so there are so many opportunities to meet someone you like.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not sure.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Not sure.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be open to meeting both internationals and Norwegians.
They have so much gluten free food, both in shops and cafes!
Remember that shops are closed on sunday and alcohol isn't sold after 18;).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Show up to the events in the first week, its a bit awkward at times, but there is some really good information and its great to meet some people.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people and seeing that you can make a life in a new place in a relatively short time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Balancing social events, studying and some alone time. I struggled a lot in the beginning, because so much is happening all the time.
But I would also say that leaving was one of the hardest parts.

questions.question: Any other comments?

questions.answer: Yes
